Divisors in projective bundles over the projective line whose complement is affine space

 

Remy van Dobben de Bruyn

 

Abstract

Given a smooth projective variety XX of dimension nn and a closed subscheme Z⊆XZ\subseteq X, it is in general a difficult problem to determine whether X∖ZX\setminus Z is isomorphic to 𝐀n\mathbf{A}^{n}. In the case where XX is a projective bundle over 𝐏1\mathbf{P}^{1} and the restriction of every irreducible component of ZZ to every fibre is a hyperplane, we give a complete geometric characterisation in terms of the irreducible components of ZZ and their intersections. In the appendix, we use this to obtain a coordinate-free explanation for the recent first counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture.

1.  Introduction

The recognition of affine spaces 𝐀n\mathbf{A}^{n} is an old and well-studied subject; see for instance [16], [13], [15], [5] for general results. In this paper, we explain a version for complements of divisors in projective bundles 𝐏⁡(ℰ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) over 𝐏1\mathbf{P}^{1} (in characteristic 00). Recalling that Pic⁡(𝐏⁡(ℰ))≅𝐙​f⊕𝐙​h\Pic(\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}))\cong\mathbf{Z}f\oplus\mathbf{Z}h where f=π∗​𝒪𝐏1​(1)f=\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^{1}}(1) is a fibre and h=𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)h=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1) is the relative tautological bundle, we prove the following result in the case of divisors whose restriction to each fibre is a hyperplane:

Theorem 1. —-

Let ℰ\mathscr{E} be a vector bundle of rank n≥2n\geq 2 on 𝐏1\mathbf{P}^{1}, and let π:X=𝐏⁡(ℰ)→𝐏1\pi\colon X=\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})\to\mathbf{P}^{1} be the projection. Let D1,…,DrD_{1},\ldots,D_{r} be pairwise distinct irreducible divisors on 𝐏⁡(ℰ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) with Di∼di​f+hD_{i}\sim d_{i}f+h for di∈𝐙d_{i}\in\mathbf{Z}, and let U=X∖(D1∪…∪Dr)U=X\setminus(D_{1}\cup\ldots\cup D_{r}). Then U≅𝐀nU\cong\mathbf{A}^{n} if and only if r=2r=2, |d2−d1|=1\lvert d_{2}-d_{1}\rvert=1, and the intersection D1∩D2D_{1}\cap D_{2} is reduced and is the union of a projective bundle of a rank n−2n-2 vector bundle with a projective space of a rank n−1n-1 vector bundle in a single fibre π−1​(p)\pi^{-1}(p).

See Theorem 3.1 and the remarks preceding it.

Relation to the Jacobian conjecture

On 19 July 2026, Levent Alpöge posted a counterexample to the three-dimensional Jacobian conjecture on the social media platform X, found using AI [1]. As explained by a comment of Andy Jiang one day later (also found using AI) [9], the example can be understood geometrically by taking a ramified cover φ:𝐏1×𝐏2→𝐏3\varphi\colon\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2}\to\mathbf{P}^{3} and removing a suitably chosen hyperplane HH (resp. the ramification divisor RR and φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H)) from the source (resp. target). It is clear that 𝐏3∖H\mathbf{P}^{3}\setminus H is isomorphic to 𝐀3\mathbf{A}^{3}, and there was a lot of online activity to understand why (𝐏1×𝐏2)∖(R∪φ−1​(H))(\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2})\setminus(R\cup\varphi^{-1}(H)) is isomorphic to 𝐀3\mathbf{A}^{3}; see for instance [11] and the blog posts [17], [18], [10], as well as the blog posts [21, 22] and expository paper [23] by the author.

When n=3n=3 and ℰ\mathscr{E} is the trivial bundle 𝒪3\mathcal{O}^{3}, the theorem above gives a criterion on RR and φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H) in order for their complement to be isomorphic to 𝐀3\mathbf{A}^{3}. In the appendix, we use Theorem 1 to show that these criteria are satisfied if and only if HH is tangent but not osculating to the small diagonal (the same condition appearing in [9])11 1 The ‘only if’ part is not difficult, but many of the online explanations do not address it, and sometimes only show the existence of a single hyperplane HH with the required properties.. In particular, this gives a coordinate-free explanation of the counterexample of [1] and [9]. We include this in the paper because it does not yet seem to appear in the published literature.

Outline of the paper

In §2, we start with some lemmas on projective bundles for which we do not know a reference, and which may be of independent interest. This is used in §3 to prove Theorem 1. The fact that the conditions on D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} are sufficient for the isomorphism with 𝐀n\mathbf{A}^{n} is a synthesis of the computations found elsewhere in relation to the counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture; see for instance the comments [9] and [11] on X, as well as the blog posts [17], [21], [22]. Thus, Theorem 1 puts this construction in a broader context.

For necessity, the exact sequence for the Picard group of an open subvariety gives the conditions r=2r=2 and |d2−d1|=1\lvert d_{2}-d_{1}\rvert=1. Computing the class of UU in the Grothendieck ring of varieties shows that D1∩D2D_{1}\cap D_{2} satisfies the conclusion, except for the reducedness statement, which is the hardest part. For this, we reduce to the case n=2n=2 using linear projection and the cancellation theorem U×𝐀n−2≅𝐀n⇒U≅𝐀2U\times\mathbf{A}^{n-2}\cong\mathbf{A}^{n}\Rightarrow U\cong\mathbf{A}^{2} [14, Ch. I, Thm. 4.2]. We then apply the criterion of Ramanujam [16] that UU should be simply connected at ∞\infty, which can be obstructed by the dual graph of the minimal SNC blowup of the pair (X,D1∪D2)(X,D_{1}\cup D_{2}) by [16, Proposition]. We show that the dual graph only meets the conditions of [loc. cit.] if D1⋅D2=1D_{1}\cdot D_{2}=1. (As we will see, this can only happen on the Hirzebruch surface 𝐅0=𝐏1×𝐏1\mathbf{F}_{0}=\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{1} and when D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} have degrees (0,1)(0,1) and (1,1)(1,1), in which case it is easy to construct an isomorphism U≅𝐀2U\cong\mathbf{A}^{2}.)

2.  Some lemmas on projective bundles

If SS is a scheme and ℱ\mathscr{F} a quasi-coherent sheaf on SS, we will write 𝐏⁡(ℱ)=𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐣S​(Sym∗⁡ℱ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})=\mathbf{Proj}_{S}(\Sym^{*}\mathscr{F}). Note that this is the projective space of 1-dimensional quotients (rather than subspaces) of ℱ\mathscr{F}: for an SS-scheme f:T→Sf\colon T\to S, morphisms T→𝐏⁡(ℱ)T\to\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F}) over SS correspond to rank 11 locally free quotients f∗​ℱ↠ℒf^{*}\mathscr{F}\twoheadrightarrow\mathscr{L} on TT [7, Prop. 4.2.3]. Likewise, we write 𝐀⁡(ℱ)\mathbf{A}(\mathscr{F}) for 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐜S​(Sym∗⁡(ℱ))\mathbf{Spec}_{S}(\Sym^{*}(\mathscr{F})), whose points on f:T→Sf\colon T\to S are given by maps f∗​ℱ→𝒪Tf^{*}\mathscr{F}\to\mathcal{O}_{T} (rather than global sections 𝒪T→f∗​ℱ\mathcal{O}_{T}\to f^{*}\mathscr{F}). Below, a vector bundle on a scheme SS will mean a locally free sheaf of finite type on SS (this is called a ‘finite locally free sheaf’ in [19, Tag 01C6]).

Lemma 2.1. —-

Let SS be a scheme, let 0→ℰ→ℱ→𝒢→00\to\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{F}\to\mathscr{G}\to 0 be a short exact sequence of quasi-coherent sheaves on SS, and let π:𝐏⁡(ℱ)→S\pi\colon\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})\to S be the projection. Then the ideal sheaf cutting out the closed immersion 𝐏⁡(𝒢)↪𝐏⁡(ℱ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G})\hookrightarrow\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F}) is the image of the composite map π∗​ℰ⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(−1)→π∗​ℱ⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(−1)↠𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)\pi^{*}\mathscr{E}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(-1)\to\pi^{*}\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(-1)\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})} induced by the tautological quotient π∗​ℱ↠𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)\pi^{*}\mathscr{F}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1). Moreover, if ℰ\mathscr{E} is invertible, then the map π∗​ℰ⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(−1)→𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)\pi^{*}\mathscr{E}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(-1)\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})} is injective.

Proof.

The map 𝐏⁡(𝒢)↪𝐏⁡(ℱ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G})\hookrightarrow\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F}) is induced by the surjection Sym∗⁡ℱ→Sym∗⁡𝒢\Sym^{*}\mathscr{F}\to\Sym^{*}\mathscr{G} of graded algebras, whose kernel is generated by the image of the map ℰ→ℱ↪Sym∗⁡ℱ\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{F}\hookrightarrow\Sym^{*}\mathscr{F} [4, Ch. III, §6, Prop. 4]. Thus, the kernel is the image of the map of quasi-coherent sheaves of graded Sym∗⁡ℱ\Sym^{*}\mathscr{F}-modules given by ℰ⁡(−1)⊗Sym∗⁡ℱ⊆ℱ⁡(−1)⊗Sym∗⁡ℱ→Sym≥1⁡ℱ\mathscr{E}(-1)\otimes\Sym^{*}\mathscr{F}\subseteq\mathscr{F}(-1)\otimes\Sym^{*}\mathscr{F}\to\Sym^{\geq 1}\mathscr{F}. Note that this composite map is injective if ℰ\mathscr{E} is invertible. The result now follows since the functor ℳ↦ℳ~\mathscr{M}\mapsto\widetilde{\mathscr{M}} from quasi-coherent sheaves of graded Sym∗⁡ℱ\Sym^{*}\mathscr{F}-modules to sheaves on 𝐏⁡(ℱ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F}) is exact and preserves Serre twists [19, Tag 01O7 and 01MT]. ∎

Lemma 2.2. —-

Let SS be a scheme, let 0→ℰ→ℱ→𝒢0\to\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{F}\to\mathscr{G} be a short exact sequence of vector bundles on SS such that ℰ\mathscr{E} has rank 11, and let X=𝐏⁡(ℱ)∖𝐏⁡(𝒢)X=\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})\setminus\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}). If f:T→Sf\colon T\to S is a morphism, then X⁡(T)X(T) is the set of splittings of the short exact sequence 0→f∗​ℰ→f∗​ℱ→f∗​𝒢→00\to f^{*}\mathscr{E}\to f^{*}\mathscr{F}\to f^{*}\mathscr{G}\to 0. In particular, XX is naturally a torsor under the SS-group scheme 𝐀⁡(ℰ−1⊗𝒢)\mathbf{A}(\mathscr{E}^{-1}\otimes\mathscr{G}).

Proof.

Given a morphism f:T→Sf\colon T\to S, a morphism g:T→𝐏⁡(ℱ)g\colon T\to\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F}) is classified by the surjection f∗​ℱ↠g∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)f^{*}\mathscr{F}\twoheadrightarrow g^{*}\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1). By Lemma 2.1, the subscheme g∗​𝐏​(𝒢)g^{*}\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}) is cut out by the image of the composite

(2.3) f∗​ℰ⊗g∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(−1)→f∗​ℱ⊗g∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(−1)↠𝒪T,f^{*}\mathscr{E}\otimes g^{*}\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(-1)\to f^{*}\mathscr{F}\otimes g^{*}\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(-1)\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{T},

so gg lands in 𝐏⁡(ℱ)∖𝐏⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})\setminus\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}) if and only if the map (2.3) is surjective. By the final statement of Lemma 2.1 and since 𝒪𝐏⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G})} is flat over SS, the map (2.3) is always injective, so 𝐏⁡(ℱ)∖𝐏⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})\setminus\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}) classifies the maps f∗​ℱ↠ℒf^{*}\mathscr{F}\twoheadrightarrow\mathscr{L} onto a line bundle such that f∗​ℰ→f∗​ℱ→ℒf^{*}\mathscr{E}\to f^{*}\mathscr{F}\to\mathscr{L} is an isomorphism. These are exactly the sections of f∗​ℰ→f∗​ℱf^{*}\mathscr{E}\to f^{*}\mathscr{F}, proving the first statement. It is clear that this is a torsor under the functor taking f:T→Sf\colon T\to S to HomT⁡(f∗​𝒢,f∗​ℰ)\Hom_{T}(f^{*}\mathscr{G},f^{*}\mathscr{E}), which in our conventions is represented by 𝐀⁡(ℰ−1⊗𝒢)\mathbf{A}(\mathscr{E}^{-1}\otimes\mathscr{G}). ∎

Lemma 2.4. —-

Let SS be an integral scheme, let ℰ\mathscr{E} be a locally free sheaf on SS of rank nn, and let X=𝐏⁡(ℰ)X=\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) with its projection π:X→S\pi\colon X\to S. Then the effective Cartier divisors DD on XX with 𝒪X​(D)≃π∗​ℒ−1⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)\mathcal{O}_{X}(D)\simeq\pi^{*}\mathscr{L}^{-1}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1) for a line bundle ℒ∈Pic⁡(S)\mathscr{L}\in\Pic(S) are given by the inclusions 𝐏⁡(ℱ)↪𝐏⁡(ℰ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})\hookrightarrow\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) induced by short exact sequences 0→ℒ→ℰ→ℱ→00\to\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{F}\to 0. If n≥2n\geq 2, then DD is irreducible if and only if ℱ\mathscr{F} is torsion-free.

Proof.

Effective Cartier divisors DD with 𝒪X​(D)≃π∗​ℒ−1⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)\mathcal{O}_{X}(D)\simeq\pi^{*}\mathscr{L}^{-1}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1) correspond to nonzero maps π∗​ℒ→𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)\pi^{*}\mathscr{L}\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1). By the adjunction π∗⊣π∗\pi^{*}\dashv\pi_{*}, these correspond to nonzero maps ℒ→π∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)≃ℰ\mathscr{L}\to\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1)\simeq\mathscr{E}, where the isomorphism is [8, Prop. 2.1.15]. Any such map is injective because SS is integral, hence corresponds to a short exact sequence

0→ℒ→ℰ→ℱ→0.0\to\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{F}\to 0.

The first statement therefore follows from Lemma 2.1. For the second, recall that Pic⁡(X)≅π∗​Pic⁡(S)⊕𝐙​h\Pic(X)\cong\pi^{*}\Pic(S)\oplus\mathbf{Z}h when n≥2n\geq 2. Thus, any expression D=D1+D2D=D_{1}+D_{2} as a sum of effective divisors has 𝒪X​(Di)≃π∗​ℒi−1⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(di)\mathcal{O}_{X}(D_{i})\simeq\pi^{*}\mathscr{L}_{i}^{-1}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(d_{i}) for some di∈𝐙d_{i}\in\mathbf{Z} and ℒi∈Pic⁡(S)\mathscr{L}_{i}\in\Pic(S). Since the DiD_{i} are effective, we get di≥0d_{i}\geq 0, so one is 00 and the other is 11. We see that DD is irreducible if and only if the map ℒ↪ℰ\mathscr{L}\hookrightarrow\mathscr{E} does not factor via a strict inclusion ℒ↪ℳ\mathscr{L}\hookrightarrow\mathscr{M} for some line bundle ℳ\mathscr{M}, which means exactly that ℱ\mathscr{F} is torsion-free. ∎

The following result is probably known, but I am not aware of a reference.

Lemma 2.5. —-

Let SS be a scheme, let 0→ℰ→ℱ→𝒢→00\to\mathscr{E}\to\mathscr{F}\to\mathscr{G}\to 0 be a short exact sequence of vector bundles on SS, and write πℰ:𝐏⁡(ℰ)→S\pi_{\mathscr{E}}\colon\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})\to S for the projection, and likewise for πℱ\pi_{\mathscr{F}} and π𝒢\pi_{\mathscr{G}}. Let ℋ\mathscr{H} be the vector bundle on 𝐏⁡(ℰ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) defined as the pushout πℰ∗ℱ⊕πℰ∗​ℰ𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)(1)\pi_{\mathscr{E}}^{*}\mathscr{F}\oplus_{\pi_{\mathscr{E}}^{*}\mathscr{E}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1). Then the blowup X~=Bl𝐏⁡(𝒢)⁡(𝐏⁡(ℱ))\widetilde{X}=\Bl_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G})}(\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})) of X=𝐏⁡(ℱ)X=\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F}) along the closed subscheme 𝐏⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}) is canonically isomorphic to the projective bundle Y=𝐏𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(ℋ)Y=\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(\mathscr{H}) over 𝐏⁡(ℰ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}), taking the exceptional divisor in X~\widetilde{X} to the divisor 𝐏𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(πℰ∗​𝒢)⊆Y\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(\pi_{\mathscr{E}}^{*}\mathscr{G})\subseteq Y.

When SS is the spectrum of a field, this is [6, Prop. 9.11] (note that [6] uses the dual convention for vector bundles), whose proof can be adapted to prove the result above for general SS under the additional hypothesis that the short exact sequence splits. One could deduce the general result from this using local splitting and glueing. Instead, we only use universal properties of projective bundles and blowups.

Proof.

We will use repeatedly and without mention that a short exact sequence of vector bundles stays exact after pullback along an arbitrary morphism of schemes. Note that ℋ\mathscr{H} sits in a commutative diagram with exact rows

(2.6)

where the left square is a pushout, which in particular shows that it is a vector bundle. Replacing SS by a clopen subscheme, we may assume that the ranks of ℰ\mathscr{E}, ℱ\mathscr{F}, and 𝒢\mathscr{G} are constant. If ℰ\mathscr{E} is zero, then 𝐏⁡(ℰ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) is empty and 𝐏⁡(ℱ)=𝐏⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})=\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}), so the blowup Bl𝐏⁡(𝒢)⁡(𝐏⁡(ℱ))\Bl_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G})}(\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})) is empty as well. If 𝒢=0\mathscr{G}=0, then 𝐏⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}) is empty and ℋ\mathscr{H} is a line bundle, so both sides are 𝐏⁡(ℰ)=𝐏⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})=\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}). Thus, we may assume that ℰ\mathscr{E} and 𝒢\mathscr{G} are both nonzero.

We have a tautological quotient πℱ∗​ℱ↠𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)\pi_{\mathscr{F}}^{*}\mathscr{F}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1), and the image of the composition πℱ∗​ℰ⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(−1)→πℱ∗​ℱ⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(−1)↠𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)\pi_{\mathscr{F}}^{*}\mathscr{E}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(-1)\to\pi_{\mathscr{F}}^{*}\mathscr{F}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(-1)\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})} is the ideal sheaf cutting out 𝐏⁡(𝒢)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{G}) by Lemma 2.1. Writing π:X~→X\pi\colon\widetilde{X}\to X for the blowup and f:X~→Sf\colon\widetilde{X}\to S for the structure map, we see that the image of the map f∗​ℰ⊗π∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(−1)→𝒪X~f^{*}\mathscr{E}\otimes\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(-1)\to\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}} is an invertible sheaf of ideals, which we will denote by ℐ\mathcal{I}. This gives a surjection f∗​ℰ↠ℐ⊗π∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)f^{*}\mathscr{E}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{I}\otimes\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1), defining a map ϕ:X~→𝐏⁡(ℰ)\phi\colon\widetilde{X}\to\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) over SS with ϕ∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)≅ℐ⊗π∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)\phi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1)\cong\mathcal{I}\otimes\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1). Then the map f∗​ℱ↠π∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)f^{*}\mathscr{F}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{\pi}^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1) factors as f∗​ℱ↠ϕ∗​ℋ↠π∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)f^{*}\mathscr{F}\twoheadrightarrow\phi^{*}\mathscr{H}\twoheadrightarrow\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1) since its restriction to f∗​ℰf^{*}\mathscr{E} lands in ϕ∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)⊆π∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)\phi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1)\subseteq\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1). This defines a morphism ϕ~:X~→Y\widetilde{\phi}\colon\widetilde{X}\to Y over 𝐏⁡(ℰ)\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) such that ϕ~∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℋ)​(1)≅π∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)\widetilde{\phi}^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{H})}(1)\cong\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1).

Conversely, write πℋ:Y→𝐏⁡(ℰ)\pi_{\mathscr{H}}\colon Y\to\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E}) and g:Y→Sg\colon Y\to S for the structure maps. We get a tautological quotient πℋ∗​ℋ↠𝒪𝐏⁡(ℋ)​(1)\pi_{\mathscr{H}}^{*}\mathscr{H}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{H})}(1), whose composition with the surjective map g∗​ℱ↠πℋ∗​ℋg^{*}\mathscr{F}\twoheadrightarrow\pi_{\mathscr{H}}^{*}\mathscr{H} defines a morphism ψ:Y→X\psi\colon Y\to X with ψ∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℱ)​(1)≅𝒪𝐏⁡(ℋ)​(1)\psi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{F})}(1)\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{H})}(1). Moreover, the map πℋ∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℋ)​(−1)→𝒪𝐏⁡(ℋ)\pi_{\mathscr{H}}^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1)\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{H})}(-1)\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{H})} is injective by Lemma 2.1 applied to the bottom sequence of (2.6). Thus, the image of the composite map

is the invertible sheaf πℋ∗​𝒪𝐏⁡(ℰ)​(1)⊗𝒪𝐏⁡(ℋ)​(−1)\pi_{\mathscr{H}}^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{E})}(1)\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}(\mathscr{H})}(-1). (This isomorphism preserves the fibre classes in Pic\Pic but adds a multiple of the fibre to hh. This change of basis does not affect our condition that d=e±1d=e\pm 1.) As in [3, Prop. IV.1], we have f2=0f^{2}=0, f⋅h=1f\cdot h=1, and h2=mh^{2}=m. Without loss of generality, we assume that e=d+1e=d+1.

First assume that k=1k=1, so 1=D⋅E=(d​f+h)⋅(e​f+h)=d+e+m1=D\cdot E=(df+h)\cdot(ef+h)=d+e+m, hence d=−m2d=-\tfrac{m}{2}. If m>0m>0, there are no effective curves in |d​f+h|\lvert df+h\rvert for −m<d<0-m<d<0, so we must have m=0m=0 and d=0d=0. Thus, DD and EE are irreducible divisors of degrees (0,1)(0,1) and (1,1)(1,1) on 𝐏1×𝐏1\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{1}. If D=𝐏1×{p}D=\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\{p\} for some p∈𝐏1p\in\mathbf{P}^{1}, then the second projection U→𝐏1∖{p}U\to\mathbf{P}^{1}\setminus\{p\} is an 𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}-bundle over 𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}, hence U≅𝐀2U\cong\mathbf{A}^{2} (this is also easily seen directly).

Conversely, suppose k>1k>1. Then DD and EE meet in a single point with multiplicity kk. Blowing up this point gives strict transforms D~\widetilde{D} and E~\widetilde{E} intersecting with multiplicity k−1k-1, and all intersection points lie on the exceptional divisor. Since DD and EE are smooth, their strict transforms meet the exceptional divisor once, so D~\widetilde{D} and E~\widetilde{E} meet in a single point with multiplicity k−1k-1. Repeating this process i<ki<k times gives strict transforms intersecting once with multiplicity k−ik-i. Finally, after kk blowups, the strict transforms D~\widetilde{D} and E~\widetilde{E} no longer meet, so the boundary divisor consisting of D~\widetilde{D}, E~\widetilde{E}, and the strict transforms of the kk exceptional divisors has simple normal crossings. Its dual graph is the Coxeter graph Dk+2D_{k+2}. Since this is not linear, [16, Proposition, and Corollary to Lemma 1] shows that UU is not simply connected at ∞\infty, and hence not isomorphic to 𝐀2\mathbf{A}^{2}. ∎

Remark 3.2. —-

When e=d±1e=d\pm 1 and WW consists of a non-reduced point, it is still true that the motive M⁡(U)M(U) is isomorphic to M⁡(𝐀n)=𝐙M(\mathbf{A}^{n})=\mathbf{Z} in DM⁡(k,𝐙)\operatorname{DM}(k,\mathbf{Z}). Indeed, the proof above gives U≅U′×𝐀n−2U\cong U^{\prime}\times\mathbf{A}^{n-2}, so we reduce to the case n=2n=2. Note that [12, 14.5.3] shows that M⁡(D∩E)=M⁡((D∩E)red)M(D\cap E)=M((D\cap E)^{\operatorname{red}}). We have M⁡(X)≅𝐙⊕𝐙⁡(1)​[2]2⊕𝐙⁡(2)​[4]M(X)\cong\mathbf{Z}\oplus\mathbf{Z}(1)[2]^{2}\oplus\mathbf{Z}(2)[4], so [12, 14.5.5] shows that M⁡(X∖(D∩E))≅𝐙⊕𝐙⁡(1)​[2]2M(X\setminus(D\cap E))\cong\mathbf{Z}\oplus\mathbf{Z}(1)[2]^{2}. Applying [12, 14.5.5] again to the smooth subscheme (D∪E)∖(D∩E)≅𝐀1∐𝐀1(D\cup E)\setminus(D\cap E)\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}\amalg\mathbf{A}^{1} inside X∖(D∩E)X\setminus(D\cap E) gives M⁡(U)≅𝐙M(U)\cong\mathbf{Z} since DD and EE form a basis for Pic⁡(X)≅Pic⁡(X∖(D∩E))\Pic(X)\cong\Pic(X\setminus(D\cap E)). In particular, any invariant that is abelian and 𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}-invariant cannot distinguish between UU and 𝐀n\mathbf{A}^{n}. (Instead, our obstruction boiled down to the non-abelian invariant given by the fundamental group at ∞\infty.)

Remark 3.3. —-

We note that Ramanujam’s obstruction in terms of dual graphs is both powerful and relatively easy to apply. I suspect that it may also be of use for studying the 22-dimensional Jacobian conjecture; I do not know if this has been attempted before.

Remark 3.4. —-

In positive characteristic, the proof that the conditions e=d±1e=d\pm 1 and length⁡(ℋtors)=1\operatorname{length}(\mathscr{H}_{\operatorname{tors}})=1 imply U≅𝐀nU\cong\mathbf{A}^{n} goes through unchanged. Conversely, the proof above shows that it is necessary that e=d±1e=d\pm 1 and ℋtors\mathscr{H}_{\operatorname{tors}} is supported on a single point. However, to show that ℋtors\mathscr{H}_{\operatorname{tors}} has to be reduced, we used a topological obstruction. It would be interesting to know whether the same conclusion can be obtained in positive characteristic.

Appendix A A coordinate-free counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture

In this appendix, we give a coordinate-free exposition of the first counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture [1], [9]. This appendix is a version of the blog post [22] and the expository paper [23] by the author. We include it here because it does not yet seem to appear in the published literature.

Definition A.1. —-

Let φ:𝐏1×Sym2⁡(𝐏1)→Sym3⁡(𝐏1)\varphi\colon\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\Sym^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1})\to\Sym^{3}(\mathbf{P}^{1}) be the map (p,{q,r})↦{p,q,r}(p,\{q,r\})\mapsto\{p,q,r\}. Let R⊆𝐏1×Sym2⁡(𝐏1)R\subseteq\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\Sym^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1}) be the ramification divisor, and let H⊆Sym3⁡(𝐏1)H\subseteq\Sym^{3}(\mathbf{P}^{1}) be a hyperplane. Let U=(𝐏1×Sym2⁡(𝐏1))∖(R∪φ−1​(H))U=(\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\Sym^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1}))\setminus(R\cup\varphi^{-1}(H)), and let V=Sym3⁡(𝐏1)∖HV=\Sym^{3}(\mathbf{P}^{1})\setminus H.

Theorem A.2 ([1, 9]). —-

If HH is tangent to order 22 to the small diagonal, then the restriction φ|U:U→V\varphi|_{U}\colon U\to V is an étale map between affine spaces of dimension 33 that is not an isomorphism.

The theory of symmetric polynomials identifies Symn⁡(𝐏1)\Sym^{n}(\mathbf{P}^{1}) with the projective space 𝐏n\mathbf{P}^{n}, so UU and VV are open subvarieties of 𝐏1×𝐏2\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2} and 𝐏3\mathbf{P}^{3} respectively. As was noted in various places (see for instance [17, 10, 21]), it is clear that V≅𝐀3V\cong\mathbf{A}^{3}, that φ|U\varphi|_{U} is étale (because we removed the ramification locus RR), and that φ|U\varphi|_{U} is not an isomorphism (since it has generic degree 33).

Thus, the content of the theorem above lies in proving that U≅𝐀3U\cong\mathbf{A}^{3} if HH is tangent to order 22 (i.e., tangent but not osculating) to the small diagonal. This can be done by explicit computation, but this does not shed light on the underlying geometry. Instead, we will deduce this from the much more general criterion of Theorem 3.1. In particular, this also provides a converse; see Theorem A.8.

We start by studying the geometry of the quotient map (𝐏1)n→Symn⁡(𝐏1)(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n}\to\Sym^{n}(\mathbf{P}^{1}), which we then use to describe the properties of the divisors RR and φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H).

A.1  Some lemmas on symmetric powers

The isomorphism U≅𝐀3U\cong\mathbf{A}^{3} in Theorem A.2 relies on the tangency of the hyperplane H⊆Sym3⁡(𝐏1)H\subseteq\Sym^{3}(\mathbf{P}^{1}) to the small diagonal. We need a local computation to extract the geometric implication of this hypothesis; see Corollary A.4 below.

By the theory of symmetric polynomials, the quotient (𝐏1)n→Symn⁡(𝐏1)(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n}\to\Sym^{n}(\mathbf{P}^{1}) is given by

π=[σ¯n:…:σ¯0]:(𝐏1)n→𝐏n,\pi=[\bar{\sigma}_{n}:\ldots:\bar{\sigma}_{0}]\colon(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n}\to\mathbf{P}^{n},

where σ¯i\bar{\sigma}_{i} is the multi-homogenised elementary symmetric polynomial

σ¯i([x1:y1],…,[xn:yn])=∑I⊆{1,…,n}|I|=i∏j∈Ixj⋅∏j∉Iyj.\bar{\sigma}_{i}([x_{1}:y_{1}],\ldots,[x_{n}:y_{n}])=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\\ \lvert I\rvert=i\end{subarray}}\prod_{j\in I}x_{j}\cdot\prod_{j\not\in I}y_{j}.

Since π\pi is homogeneous of degree (1,…,1)(1,\ldots,1), we get π∗​𝒪𝐏n​(1)≃𝒪(𝐏1)n​(1,…,1)\pi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^{n}}(1)\simeq\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n}}(1,\ldots,1). We also note that the image of the small diagonal in (𝐏1)n(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n} gives (a slightly reparametrised version of) the rational normal curve ι:𝐏1→𝐏n\iota\colon\mathbf{P}^{1}\to\mathbf{P}^{n}, where the ii-th coordinate is (ni)​xn−i​yi\binom{n}{i}x^{n-i}y^{i}. We denote the image of ι\iota by CC.

Given a subset I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} and p∈𝐏1p\in\mathbf{P}^{1}, write ΔI\Delta_{I} (resp. ΔI,p\Delta_{I,p}) for the closed subset of tuples (p1,…,pn)∈(𝐏1)n(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})\in(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n} such that pi=pjp_{i}=p_{j} for all i,j∈Ii,j\in I (resp. pi=pp_{i}=p for all i∈Ii\in I). If I={i1,…,ik}I=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}, we also write Δi1​…​ik\Delta_{i_{1}\ldots i_{k}} for ΔI\Delta_{I}. For i∈{0,…,n}i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, write Δ(i)\Delta_{(i)} (resp. Δ(i),p\Delta_{(i),p}) for the union of ΔI\Delta_{I} (resp. ΔI,p\Delta_{I,p}) over all sets I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} with |I|=i\lvert I\rvert=i. Note that Δ(i)\Delta_{(i)} (resp. Δ(i),p\Delta_{(i),p}) is the subscheme of nn-tuples (p1,…,pn)(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}) where at least ii of the coordinates agree (resp. are equal to pp).

Lemma A.3. —-

Let π:(𝐏1)n→𝐏n\pi\colon(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n}\to\mathbf{P}^{n} be the map above. Then Δ(i+1),[0:1]\Delta_{(i+1),[0:1]} is the preimage of the linear subspace {[x0:…:xn]|x0=…=xi=0}\{[x_{0}:\ldots:x_{n}]\ |\ x_{0}=\ldots=x_{i}=0\}.

Proof.

The coordinates ([x1:y1],…,[xn:yn])([x_{1}:y_{1}],\ldots,[x_{n}:y_{n}]) in (𝐏1)n(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n} satisfy the relation

∑i=0nσ¯n−iTi=(x1+y1T)⋯(xn+ynT).\sum_{i=0}^{n}\bar{\sigma}_{n-i}T^{i}=(x_{1}+y_{1}T)\cdots(x_{n}+y_{n}T).

The left hand side shows that σ¯n=…=σ¯n−i=0\bar{\sigma}_{n}=\ldots=\bar{\sigma}_{n-i}=0 if and only if this polynomial is divisible by Ti+1T^{i+1}, which by examining the right hand side means exactly that at least i+1i+1 of the coordinates are equal to [0:1][0:1]. ∎

Corollary A.4. —-

A hyperplane H⊆𝐏nH\subseteq\mathbf{P}^{n} is tangent to CC to order ≥i\geq i at pp if and only if π−1​(H)\pi^{-1}(H) contains the locus Δ(n−i+1),p\Delta_{(n-i+1),p} where at least n−i+1n-i+1 of the coordinates are equal to pp.

Proof.

Applying a coordinate transformation, we may assume p=[0:1]p=[0:1]. If HH is given by a0​x0+…+an​xn=0a_{0}x_{0}+\ldots+a_{n}x_{n}=0, then its pullback along the rational normal curve 𝐏1→𝐏n\mathbf{P}^{1}\to\mathbf{P}^{n} is given by ∑i=0nai​(ni)​xn−i​yi\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}\binom{n}{i}x^{n-i}y^{i}, so it is tangent to order ≥i\geq i at [0:1][0:1] if and only if an=…=an−i+1=0a_{n}=\ldots=a_{n-i+1}=0. This means that HH contains the linear subspace V⁡(x0,…,xn−i)V(x_{0},\ldots,x_{n-i}), which by Lemma A.3 means that π−1​(H)\pi^{-1}(H) contains the locus where at least n−i+1n-i+1 of the coordinates are equal to pp. ∎

Lemma A.5. —-

Let H⊆𝐏nH\subseteq\mathbf{P}^{n} be a hyperplane that is tangent to CC to order i≥1i\geq 1 at pp, and let I⊆{1,…,n}I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} be a subset of size n−i+1n-i+1. Then π−1​(H)∩ΔI\pi^{-1}(H)\cap\Delta_{I} is reduced along ΔI,p\Delta_{I,p}.

Proof.

Note that π−1​(H)∩ΔI\pi^{-1}(H)\cap\Delta_{I} contains ΔI,p\Delta_{I,p} by Corollary A.4. Without loss of generality, assume p=[0:1]p=[0:1] and I={i,…,n}I=\{i,\ldots,n\}. Write ρ\rho for the composition ΔI↪(𝐏1)n→𝐏n\Delta_{I}\hookrightarrow(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n}\to\mathbf{P}^{n}, and note that ι:𝐏1→𝐏n\iota\colon\mathbf{P}^{1}\to\mathbf{P}^{n} factors via 𝐏1→ΔI→𝐏n\mathbf{P}^{1}\to\Delta_{I}\to\mathbf{P}^{n} (in fact, via the small diagonal Δ{1,…,n}⊂(𝐏1)n\Delta_{\{1,\ldots,n\}}\subset(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{n}). If HH is given by a0​x0+…+an​xn=0a_{0}x_{0}+\ldots+a_{n}x_{n}=0, then π−1​(H)\pi^{-1}(H) is given by a0​σ¯n+…+an​σ¯0=0a_{0}\bar{\sigma}_{n}+\ldots+a_{n}\bar{\sigma}_{0}=0, and ρ−1​(H)\rho^{-1}(H) is obtained from this by setting xi=…=xnx_{i}=\ldots=x_{n} and yi=…=yny_{i}=\ldots=y_{n}. By assumption, we have an=…=an−i+1=0a_{n}=\ldots=a_{n-i+1}=0 and an−i≠0a_{n-i}\neq 0. Note that ΔI,p\Delta_{I,p} is cut out in ΔI\Delta_{I} by xix_{i}, so we need to show that the equation for ρ−1​(H)\rho^{-1}(H) is not divisible by xi2x_{i}^{2}. The pullback

Γ⁡(𝐏n,𝒪⁡(1))\displaystyle\Gamma(\mathbf{P}^{n},\mathcal{O}(1)) →Γ⁡(𝐏1,ι∗​𝒪​(1))=Γ⁡(𝐏1,𝒪⁡(n))\displaystyle\to\Gamma(\mathbf{P}^{1},\iota^{*}\mathcal{O}(1))=\Gamma(\mathbf{P}^{1},\mathcal{O}(n))
xi\displaystyle x_{i} ↦(ni)​xn−i​yi\displaystyle\mapsto\tbinom{n}{i}x^{n-i}y^{i}

is injective, so the same goes for the pullback Γ⁡(𝐏n,𝒪⁡(1))→Γ⁡(ΔI,ρ∗​𝒪​(1))\Gamma(\mathbf{P}^{n},\mathcal{O}(1))\to\Gamma(\Delta_{I},\rho^{*}\mathcal{O}(1)). Thus, to show that the equation for ρ−1​(H)\rho^{-1}(H) is not divisible by xi2x_{i}^{2}, it suffices to show that one of its terms aj​σ¯n−ja_{j}\bar{\sigma}_{n-j} isn’t. The term an−i​σ¯ia_{n-i}\bar{\sigma}_{i} is given by an−i​∑|J|=i∏j∈Jxj⋅∏j∉Jyja_{n-i}\sum_{\lvert J\rvert=i}\prod_{j\in J}x_{j}\cdot\prod_{j\not\in J}y_{j}. Setting xi=…=xnx_{i}=\ldots=x_{n} and yi=…=yny_{i}=\ldots=y_{n}, we see that all terms are divisible by xix_{i} (since J∩I≠∅J\cap I\neq\varnothing for all JJ with |J|=i\lvert J\rvert=i), but the term for J={1,…,i}J=\{1,\ldots,i\} is not divisible by xi2x_{i}^{2}. ∎

A.2  Geometric properties of the boundary divisors

To study (𝐏1×𝐏2)∖(R∪φ−1​(H))(\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2})\setminus(R\cup\varphi^{-1}(H)), we first give a geometric description of the boundary divisors RR and φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H), as well as their intersection R∩φ−1​(H)R\cap\varphi^{-1}(H).

Lemma A.6. —-

The divisor RR is irreducible of degree (2,1)(2,1), and its pullback to (𝐏1)3(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{3} is the union of pairwise diagonals Δ12∪Δ13\Delta_{12}\cup\Delta_{13}.

Proof.

The cover (𝐏1)3→𝐏3(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{3}\to\mathbf{P}^{3} is ramified along the union of the pairwise diagonals Δi​j\Delta_{ij}, which each have ramification index 22 since their inertia subgroups are ⟨(i​j)⟩\langle(ij)\rangle. Using multiplicativity of ramification indices [19, Tag 0BRL], we see that the preimage of RR in (𝐏1)3(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{3} is Δ12∪Δ13\Delta_{12}\cup\Delta_{13}, which has degree (1,1,0)+(1,0,1)=(2,1,1)(1,1,0)+(1,0,1)=(2,1,1). Thus, RR has degree (2,1)(2,1), since the pullback of 𝒪𝐏2​(1)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^{2}}(1) to (𝐏1)2(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{2} is 𝒪(𝐏1)2​(1,1)\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{2}}(1,1). Since the Galois group of (𝐏1)3→𝐏1×𝐏2(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{3}\to\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2} interchanges the two components of Δ12∪Δ13\Delta_{12}\cup\Delta_{13}, we see that RR is irreducible. ∎

Given a subscheme Z⊆𝐏1×𝐏2Z\subseteq\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2} and a point p∈𝐏1p\in\mathbf{P}^{1}, we will write Zp⊆𝐏2Z_{p}\subseteq\mathbf{P}^{2} for the fibre Z∩({p}×𝐏2)Z\cap(\{p\}\times\mathbf{P}^{2}) above pp.

Lemma A.7. —-

The divisor φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H) has degree (1,1)(1,1). Given a point p∈𝐏1p\in\mathbf{P}^{1}, the fibre φ−1​(H)p\varphi^{-1}(H)_{p} equals RpR_{p} (resp. 𝐏2\mathbf{P}^{2}) if and only if HH is tangent to order 22 (resp. 33) at pp. In the degree 22 case, the intersection R∩φ−1​(H)R\cap\varphi^{-1}(H) is reduced along φ−1​(H)p=Rp\varphi^{-1}(H)_{p}=R_{p}.

Proof.

The degree statement follows since the pullback of 𝒪𝐏1×𝐏2​(a,b)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2}}(a,b) along the quotient map (𝐏1)3→𝐏1×𝐏2(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{3}\to\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2} is 𝒪(𝐏1)3​(a,b,b)\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{3}}(a,b,b), and π−1​(H)\pi^{-1}(H) has degree (1,1,1)(1,1,1). To see whether the fibre of φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H) agrees with that of RR or 𝐏1×𝐏2\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2}, it suffices to check this after pulling back along the map g:(𝐏1)3→𝐏1×𝐏2g\colon(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{3}\to\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2}. Now Lemma A.6 gives g∗​R=Δ12∪Δ13g^{*}R=\Delta_{12}\cup\Delta_{13}, whose fibre above pp is ({p}×𝐏1)∪(𝐏1×{p})(\{p\}\times\mathbf{P}^{1})\cup(\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\{p\}). On the other hand, by Corollary A.4, the pullback of HH to {p}×(𝐏1)2\{p\}\times(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{2} contains ({p}×𝐏1)∪(𝐏1×{p})(\{p\}\times\mathbf{P}^{1})\cup(\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\{p\}) (resp. equals (𝐏1)2(\mathbf{P}^{1})^{2}) if and only if HH is tangent to order ≥2\geq 2 (resp. ≥3\geq 3) at pp. In the order 22 case, the inclusion Rp↪φ−1​(H)pR_{p}\hookrightarrow\varphi^{-1}(H)_{p} is an equality since both are effective divisors of degree 11 on 𝐏2\mathbf{P}^{2}. For the reducedness statement, it suffices to check this after pulling back along gg [19, Tag 06QM], where the result follows from Lemma A.5. ∎

Theorem A.8. —-

The complement U=𝐏1×𝐏2∖(R∪φ−1​(H))U=\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2}\setminus(R\cup\varphi^{-1}(H)) is isomorphic to 𝐀3\mathbf{A}^{3} if and only if HH is tangent but not osculating to the small diagonal.

Proof.

By Lemma A.6 and Lemma A.7, the divisors RR and φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H) have degrees (2,1)(2,1) and (1,1)(1,1) respectively. If HH is osculating to the small diagonal (i.e., tangent to order 33) at a point pp, then φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H) contains {p}×𝐏2\{p\}\times\mathbf{P}^{2} by Lemma A.7, hence is reducible. Then the components of RR and φ−1​(H)\varphi^{-1}(H) cannot form a basis of Pic⁡(𝐏1×𝐏2)\Pic(\mathbf{P}^{1}\times\mathbf{P}^{2}), so UU is not isomorphic to 𝐀3\mathbf{A}^{3}. In all other cases, HH does not contain a vertical fibre {p}×𝐏2\{p\}\times\mathbf{P}^{2}, hence is irreducible by Lemma 2.4. By Lemma A.6, we know that RR is irreducible. By Theorem 3.1, we see that U≅𝐀3U\cong\mathbf{A}^{3} if and only if R∩φ−1​(H)R\cap\varphi^{-1}(H) is a union of a section and a reduced line {p}×L\{p\}\times L in a vertical fibre. By Lemma A.7, this happens if and only if HH is tangent to the small diagonal at a point pp (of which there can be at most one since HH intersects the small diagonal with multiplicity 33). ∎

Remark A.9. —-

The hardest part of the proof of Theorem 3.1 is the verification that D∩ED\cap E needs to be reduced if U≅𝐀nU\cong\mathbf{A}^{n}. For Theorem A.8, we only needed the easier obstruction that ℋtors\mathscr{H}_{\operatorname{tors}} needs to be supported in a single point, plus the construction of an isomorphism with 𝐀n\mathbf{A}^{n} in the case where D∩ED\cap E is reduced (which is also easy). Thus, we do not need the full strength of Theorem 3.1 — see for instance [21, 22] for arguments along this line.

In particular, by Remark 3.4, we see that Theorem A.8 also holds in positive characteristic. (We note that the Jacobian conjecture was already known to be false in positive characteristic due to the existence of Artin–Schreier covers 𝐀1→𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}\to\mathbf{A}^{1}. Thus, a possible positive result would require further restrictions on the map, such as tame ramification at ∞\infty.)
